cards.title: Larry Seese
cards.prompt: Seese blamed the collapse on a change AT&T had made deliberately, as an improvement, the month before. Name the improvement, and say what property of it turned one switch's recovery into a nationwide cascade.
cards.body: The man who had to explain it. A week after the outage he walked the trade journal Telephony through the mechanism switch by switch — the deliberate speed-up, the second message, the shutdown, the chain reaction. "The fault was in the code" of the update loaded into all 114 4ESS switches in mid-December.
cards.answer: They sped up how a switch learns its neighbour is back. Before, switch A sent an explicit 'I am working again' and B double-checked. After, B inferred it from A's first SS7 initial address message — an ordinary call attempt. The status update was now driven by production traffic, so a recovering switch's own calls became the trigger, and every switch ran that same code.

cards.title: AT&T's nine-hour Monday
cards.sub: 15 January 1990 · 4ESS toll network, coast to coast
cards.prompt: AT&T's engineers reached for their standard recovery procedures first, and the report says these "proved inadequate". Explain why every standard procedure made it worse, and what the one move that finally worked had in common with doing nothing.
cards.body: One New York 4ESS hit a minor hardware fault at 2:30 p.m. EST and began a normal four-to-six second recovery. The effect cascaded: Direct Link Node processors in other switches went out of service too, and stayed unstable because traffic kept supplying the triggers. Last link cleared 11:30 p.m. EST; rollback next day. Monday's calling volume was below normal.
cards.answer: Standard procedures restore switches to service, and a switch returning to service is exactly what emits the paired call attempts that damage its neighbours' Direct Link Node processors — recovery was the propagation mechanism. The move that worked was subtractive: suspending signalling traffic on the backup links cut the message rate below the density that produced two attempts within 1/100th of a second, so the oscillation damped instead of feeding itself.

cards.title: Technical background on AT&T's network slowdown
cards.prompt: The report names what the mid-December update was actually for. Say what it was meant to improve — then say why that purpose makes this a worse failure than an ordinary bug shipped to the whole fleet.
cards.body: AT&T's own account, released through its Consultant Liaison Program and reproduced in ACM RISKS Digest Volume 9 Issue 63. It names the Direct Link Node processor, its duplicated mate, the several-second vulnerable window and the 1/100th-of-a-second couplet inside it, and the mid-December update that put the flaw into every 4ESS at once. It is short; go and read it.
cards.answer: The update was "intended to significantly improve the network's performance by making it possible for switching systems to access a backup signaling network more quickly in case of problems with the main CCS7 signaling network." The failover path itself was the thing running identically in every 4ESS switch in the network, so the duplicated mate inside the switch and the switches a continent away shared the defect equally — and the network was finally stabilised by suspending signalling on those same backup links.

cards.title: A system problem, not a component problem
cards.prompt: AT&T duplicated the processor that joins each switch to the signalling network, and spread 114 switches across a continent — and both walls failed the same way. Murray refused the obvious reading of that. Name the category he put the failure in instead, and state the property that decides whether a boundary you draw will hold.
cards.body: Thirteen days after the outage, in the digest issue that carried AT&T's report, Murray refused the component reading: "It was not a COMPONENT problem; it was, as I feared and suggested a SYSTEM problem." He added two rules: avoid gratuitous automation, and if you cannot test it, do not do it.
cards.answer: A SYSTEM problem — the failure lived in what every component had in common, not in any one component. The modern reading, which is yours to draw and not Murray's words: a wall only contains a failure that cannot cross it, so a cell's blast radius is set by the most-shared thing inside it — same build, same config, same control plane. Geography is not a boundary; not sharing is.
